name: Agreement with the Capote, Muache and Weeminuche bands of Ute, 1878 (Pagosa Springs, never ratified)
citation: Agreement of November 9, 1878 (not ratified; superseded by the agreement of March 6, 1880)
nations: Southern Ute Indian Tribe (Muache and Capote bands)
promises: The Muache, Capote and Weeminuche bands would give up their rights in the Confederated Ute reservation in Colorado set apart by the treaty of 1868, especially its southern part.
The United States would set apart a reservation for them on the San Juan River in Colorado and establish an Indian agency there in 1879.

breaches.what: Congress took no action to ratify this agreement. It was superseded on March 6, 1880 by another agreement, amended and ratified by Congress on June 15, 1880.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

source.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule p. 893

breaches.quote: No action was taken by Congress ratifying this agreement.

today: The reservation promised was set apart by executive order of February 7, 1879 and restored to the public domain by executive order of August 4, 1882 (Royce).

openQuestions: Royce says the Yampa, Grand River, Uinta and Tabeguache bands concurred in the cession; the Oklahoma State catalog lists them as signatories too. The Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation is not in presentDayTribes.
The Oklahoma State record cites 20 Stat. 396 for this agreement; that citation was not opened, so what Congress did at that page is not settled.
The Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute tribes' own accounts of the 1878 agreement were not found in this pass.

plain.promised: The Muache, Capote and Weeminuche Ute would give up their part of the 1868 Ute reservation, and the United States would set apart a new reservation for them on the San Juan River.
plain.happened: Congress never ratified the agreement. It was replaced by the agreement of March 6, 1880.
plain.today: The reservation set apart under it in 1879 was returned to the public domain in 1882.
